title: Words Hidden in Order Inside a Text
statement:
You get a lowercase string text and a list of lowercase words. A word is hidden in the text if you can delete some letters of text (possibly none) and read the word from what is left, without reordering anything. In other words, the word is a subsequence of the text.

Return how many entries of words are hidden in text. If the same word appears several times in the list, each copy counts.

examples.why: "pat", "net" and "plan" can be read left to right. "tan" uses letters that exist, but the only "t" comes after the "a" and "n".
Both copies of "ab" count. "aaa" needs three a's and the text has two.

constraints: text and words[i] contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Checking one word is easy: walk the text and match the word's letters greedily. The problem is doing that for 5000 words over a 50 000-letter text.
Either avoid rescanning the text per word, for example by storing the positions of each letter and binary-searching for the next one, or scan the text only once for all words at the same time.

Single pass: put every word in a bucket keyed by the next letter it needs. For each letter of the text, take that letter's bucket, advance each word by one letter, and move it to the bucket of its new next letter. Words that run out of letters are hidden.

explain.intuition:
For one word, greedy matching works: take the earliest possible match for each letter, because an earlier match leaves more of the text for the rest. Doing that per word rereads the text up to 5000 times, though, and a word that fails at its last letter rereads all of it.

Flip the loop. Read the text once, and keep every word waiting for its next letter, like event listeners registered by event type. When the text produces a letter, only the words waiting for that letter wake up, advance one step, and re-register for their next letter. Each word letter is handled once, so the total cost is the text length plus the total word length.
steps: Create 26 buckets. For each word, add a cursor (wordIndex, 0) to the bucket of its first letter.
For each letter c of text, take the whole bucket for c and empty it.
Advance each cursor in it by one. If it reached the end of its word, count it. Otherwise add it to the bucket of the word's next letter.
pitfalls: Re-adding a cursor to the same bucket you are iterating over, so it advances twice on one text letter ("aa" would match the text "a"). Swap the bucket out before processing it.
Deduplicating the words list. Repeated words must each be counted.
Checking only that the word's letters exist in the text, ignoring order, like "tan" in the first example.

solutions.title: Greedy scan per word
solutions.idea: For each word, walk the text once and match its letters in order.

solutions.title: Letter positions + binary search
solutions.idea: Store the sorted positions of each letter. For each letter of a word, binary-search the first position after the previous match.

solutions.title: One pass with waiting buckets
solutions.idea: Every word waits in the bucket of its next needed letter. Each text letter advances exactly the words waiting for it.

followups: The text stays the same and words arrive one at a time over a long session. Which of the three methods would you use, and what do you precompute?
Instead of a yes/no per word, return the shortest prefix of the text that contains each word as a subsequence.
